Linear Algebra for Data Science: Vectors & Matrices

Written by Ashok Kumar Yadav

Xenors founder and technical writer. View author profile · Editorial policy · How we verify

Learn vectors, matrices, dot products, matrix multiplication, eigenvalues and why linear algebra matters in machine learning.

By Ashok Kumar YadavHands-on examples + practiceDataset + notebook included

Learn vectors, matrices, dot products, matrix multiplication, eigenvalues and why linear algebra matters in machine learning. Work through the matrix and vector methods examples in order, then change one assumption and explain whether your interpretation still holds. This page targets the practical intent behind matrix and vector methods, not repetition of the phrase itself.

Editorial note: Publication metadata for Linear Algebra for Data Science is intentionally unset until this URL is actually released; the lesson already includes its own examples, CSV and notebook.

Interpret matrix and vector methods before reaching for a formula

In linear regression, predictions can be written compactly as Xw: the feature matrix X multiplied by the parameter vector w.

  • Vectors represent ordered quantities, matrices organize transformations and datasets, and matrix multiplication composes linear operations.
  • Dot products measure alignment and appear in projections, similarity and neural-network layers.
  • Eigenvectors identify directions preserved by a linear transformation, while eigenvalues describe the scaling along those directions.
  • Shape checking is essential: many linear-algebra bugs are dimension mismatches disguised by broadcasting.

Calculate a small case and verify it in Python

For matrix and vector methods, predict one visible result before each snippet runs—a row count, shape, statistic, ranking or error pattern—then compare it with the printed checkpoint.

Example 1 · Baseline example
# matrix and vector methods · example 1
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 5], [1, 8]], dtype=float)
w = np.array([10, 3], dtype=float)
y_hat = X @ w
print(y_hat)
Output / checkpoint
matrix and vector methods checkpoint 1: Run the cell and inspect the printed values before changing anything.
Example 2 · Summarize the sample
# matrix and vector methods · example 2
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv('practice.csv')
x = df.select_dtypes('number').iloc[:,0].dropna()
print('n=', len(x), 'mean=', round(x.mean(),2), 'median=', round(x.median(),2))
Output / checkpoint
matrix and vector methods checkpoint 2: n, mean and median are printed from the first numeric column.
Example 3 · Measure spread
# matrix and vector methods · example 3
q1, q3 = x.quantile([0.25,0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
print('std=', round(x.std(ddof=1),2), 'IQR=', round(iqr,2))
Output / checkpoint
matrix and vector methods checkpoint 3: Standard deviation and IQR provide two different views of spread.
Example 4 · Bootstrap one statistic
# matrix and vector methods · example 4
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
boot = [rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(1000)]
print(np.percentile(boot,[2.5,50,97.5]).round(2))
Output / checkpoint
matrix and vector methods checkpoint 4: The three values are the bootstrap 2.5th, 50th and 97.5th percentiles.
Example 5 · Check sensitivity to an extreme value
# matrix and vector methods · example 5
x2 = pd.concat([x, pd.Series([x.max()*5])], ignore_index=True)
print('mean change:', round(x2.mean()-x.mean(),2))
print('median change:', round(x2.median()-x.median(),2))
Output / checkpoint
matrix and vector methods checkpoint 5: The mean usually moves more than the median when one extreme value is added.
